title: Clay reclaim from trimmings
subtitle: Reclaiming dried clay scraps back to workable condition
excerpt: Clay trimmings, slab offcuts, and greenware that didn't work out can all be reclaimed to workable clay. The reclaim process for air-dry clay returns it to a usable state without the wedging required for kiln-fired clay. This tutorial covers the slake-and-dry-back method used to reclaim small amounts of air-dry clay from workshop scraps.
sourceNotes: Clay reclaim methodology adapted for air-dry clay from standard kiln-clay reclaim practice. Slake-and-dry-back is the foundational reclaim process documented across ceramics instruction literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Unfired clay in any stage of drying. Greenware that has not fully hardened can be reclaimed by slaking in water.
To dissolve dry or semi-dry clay back into a slurry by soaking in water. The first step in the reclaim process.
Kneading and folding clay to homogenise moisture, remove air pockets, and align clay particles before building or throwing.

content.text: Air-dry clay that has dried out but has not yet fully hardened (still white-to-cream, not yellowed or brittle) can be returned to workable clay by slaking. Clay that has fully hardened and set permanently: past the point where it crumbles to white powder in your hands: cannot be reclaimed with water: the clay particles have undergone a final bond. Limit reclaim to
Break scraps into pieces no larger than 3 cm and place in a bucket. Cover completely with water and leave to
: 2 to 4 hours for leather-hard scraps, overnight for dry scraps. Do not stir; allow the clay to dissolve in its own time.

Once slaked to a smooth slurry with no visible lumps, pour off excess water from the top of the bucket (do not pour the clay down a drain: the fine clay particles set in the pipes). The remaining slurry should be thick enough to hold a spoon upright briefly.

Pour the slurry into a shallow container: a plaster bat if available, or a large flat plastic tray or baking dish lined with a damp cloth. A plaster bat absorbs water quickly and speeds up the dry-back significantly. A plastic tray takes longer but works without specialist equipment.

Leave uncovered in a warm room. Check every hour. The surface will form a skin as moisture evaporates from the top. When the edges start to look dry and the centre is still damp, flip the slab over to dry the underside.
When the clay is firm and workable, peel it from the tray. Give it a brief
— a short knead — to even out the moisture before building.

Air-dry clay that has fully set and hardened (yellowed or browning; crumbles to dust when squeezed) cannot be returned to workable clay by soaking: the setting reaction is irreversible. Dispose of these scraps in general waste; do not pour clay liquid down drains.
Reclaimed clay is sticky and not workable after drying back: insufficient dry-back time. Allow more time; the clay needs to lose more water.
Reclaimed clay has lumps that won't dissolve: some scraps were too far into the setting process and could not slake. Remove these lumps before pouring the slurry.
Mixing clay bodies in the reclaim bucket: keep only one clay body per reclaim bucket. Mixed clay bodies have incompatible shrinkage rates and produce clay that cracks more readily.

rows.problem: Dry-back taking more than a day
rows.cause: Slurry too wet; container too deep; environment cool and humid
rows.fix: Pour off more standing water before dry-back. Use a shallower container. Move to a warmer, drier spot.

rows.problem: Reclaimed clay has inconsistent texture: some sections hard, some soft
rows.cause: Uneven drying across the slab during dry-back
rows.fix: Wedge thoroughly for longer than fresh clay. Cut the clay mass in half and check: if still visibly different in texture, fold and wedge again.
